Hi Zhian,

Thanks so much for your reply. I have a couple of questions now! So the first step in that guide you linked is to give xvalDapc() a go, but I am unsure of what the actual input is? I see in the tutorial it is 'nancycats' but for real data what would you suggest?

I also tried a dapc() command with `NULL` for n.pca and n.da, and made the following scatter plot with the code: scatter(bbel1.dapc, col = cols, cex = 2, legend = TRUE, clabel = F, posi.leg = "bottomleft", scree.pca = TRUE, posi.pca = "topleft", cleg = 0.75)

So would I call that the result of my "exploratory analysis"? It gave me some PCA values to look at an DA eingenvalues, and I'd like to keep going with my analyses. I feel like I might be pretty close, but I'd love to get something like that cross-validation plot done for the data to confirm it. Thanks so much again!!

On Monday, April 26, 2021 at 6:32:25 PM UTC-5 zka...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hello,
>
> The confusion is COMPLETELY understandable (especially for documentation that was written before I was in grad school). The values of n.pca and n.da MUST be obtained through exploratory analysis (e.g. leave the n.pca and n.da arguments blank the first time). The key is that you are creating a model of your data and you want to balance the signal and the noise.
>
> The number of PCs are determined by the number of alleles in a data set. The more alleles, the more PCs you have to choose from. If you choose all of them, then your discriminant analysis will perfectly fit the posterior group assignments to your data, which is a bit like drawing a line that connects all the dots in a linear regression. To help choose the right number, you can use cross-validation: https://grunwaldlab.github.io/Population_Genetics_in_R/DAPC.html#cross-validation-dapc-analysis-of-phytophthora-ramorum-from-forests-and-nurseries
>
> The justification for choosing the number of DA is similar: you want a model to represent your grouping data, but you don't want it to overfit your data. This is where the DA graph comes in (during exploratory analysis). The higher the bars on the graph, the more variance they explain. The lower bars often represent more noise than anything. This becomes important when you want to create one of those structure-like plots with compoplot(), because that uses all the information from the DA to create that graph. If you over-fit, then you are bundling the noise in your result.
>
> I hope that helps.
>
> All the best,
> Zhian
>
> On Monday, April 12, 2021 at 9:28:31 PM UTC-7 tau...@illinois.edu wrote:
> > Hi all,
> >
> > As the title says, I'm working with the dapc() function in RStudio and am struggling a little bit to understand n.pca and n.da in the function. I've read a few guides online, and honestly the numbers the authors use each time really confuses the heck out of me (which is my fault, not theirs!). I guess I have one simple question: how in the world do you find the best values for n.pca and n.da?
> >
> > In my glPca() function, I have an nf of 5 for my samples (I have SNP data of 55 individuals across 5 countries), and am wondering if that is part of what is used for those two variables? It's probably obvious (lol it for sure is), but I'm pretty new to this stuff, but I am trying!
> >
> > Thanks so much,
> >

messages.subject_clean: questions about results from the adegenet server
messages.body_plain:
Hi-
Basically, this set of questions are:  why did the adegenetServer give me different results than running dapc() itself? .

First: how I did the analysis:
I have been looking at the number of subpopulations in my bird data set: 64 individuals, 3529 SNPs.  I had lots more SNPs but removed all those that had any missing data.

I ran find.clusters() retaining 30 to 60 pcs in 5 pc steps, using both the kmeans and the ward clustering methods.  Ward seemed to work better, but both methods gave 4 groups when 35 or 40 pcs were retained and they seemed reasonable.

When I ran dapc() I always put in for n.pca the number of pcs I had retained in the find.clusters step (40 in this case).
QUESTION1:  Is that the right choice n.pca for the dapc computation?
QUESTION2:  the number of discriminant function eigenvalues had two of the eigenvalues much larger than the 3d, so I kept only 2.  IS that right, or should I have kept all 3?

When I then looked at the posterior membership probabilities, for the particular run I am concerned about I saw that group members of 2 of the 4 groups had 100% membership probability---that's fine.  For members of the other 2 groups they had membership probabilities partly in one group and partly in the other---no problem.
Running assignplot seemed to agree with memberships.

Here is where I have the big question: I don't seem to get the same results when I run the adegenet server:

I executed: adegenetServer(what=c("DAPC"))
and looked at the compoplot.  ****When I put in 40 for the "number of PCA axes retained", I got a plot with 100% group membership for each of individuals for each of the 4 groups!  *** Not partial memberships for those in the 2 mixed groups.***
However, when I instead checked the box for "Use suggested number of PCA components" ***I got the correct 100% memberships when I should have and partial memberships for the others---just like posterior membership probabilities!*** But the "suggested number of PCAs" was only 5, not 40!  And when I ran cross validation with 100 steps, the value of 40 came out as the right one to use.
QUESTION3:  why didn't using 40 for the compoplot calculation work?

QUESTION4: If I say that I used 3 (all) of the DA axes instead of 2, the plot changed.  Here's why I wonder if I should always use all of the discriminants rather than ignoring the 3d small one.

Thank you very much! DAPC appears to be just what I need for my analysis, but getting different results with the adegenetServer makes me question what's right and what's wrong.

Regards

Janice Boyd
Texas A&M University

messages.body_plain:
Hi Zhian:
Thank you for your earlier response on a strange result using the adegenet Server.  But now I have another question regarding use of find_clusters and the results I get using different numbers of retained pc's.
Setting is:  My dataset has 63 (diploid) individuals, 3529 loci.

I ran find.clusters with 50 and 60 retained pcs and, the number of clusters according to the BIC values were both 2. (Plot starting near 1 or 2 and consistently rising--no actual minimum)

The rest of the dapc analysis gives results that are reasonable.  The separation of the individuals on a PC2vsPC1 plot looks reasonable. The two clusters have (significant) pairwise Fst of 0.16.

But running find.clusters retaining 40, 35, or 30 pcs gives very nice BIC plots showing a minimum of 4 populations. Running the rest of the dapc analysis USING 40 (or whatever) RETAINED PCs always gives 4 very reasonable populations that on a PC2vsPC1 plot shows  upper and lower populations that are "pure" on the compoplot, and 2 populations located between the upper and lower ones that show themselves in the compoplot as being made up of correspondingly greater and lesser fractions of the main populations. Pairwise Fst's are significant and on the order of .025, .008, .026, .020, .047.

Does this imply:  there are two main populations, but the individuals actually occur in two separate pure populations  and 2 mixed populations located inbetween?  Unfortunately I have no geographic locations for the samples but this would make biological sense

Supporting my interpretation is that an earlier study using microsatellites with samples from the same general geographic area also found using STRUCTURE a peak at 2 (or 1) populations and a second lower peak at 4 populations.  Again, no geographic information available. My STRUCTURE runs gave a variety of populations (6, 4, 2, 3) but the data violate just about every assumption for STRUCTURE so I don't believe the outputs. (with days of computation vs seconds for dapc)

Before I write this up in a paper I'd like commentary from you regarding if my interpretation is reasonable or way off base.

Thank you very much for your thoughts.

Regards
Janice Boyd
Texas A&M University
